facts.quote: The Wine Centre is situated at the eastern end of North Terrace, Adelaide in the east parklands and adjacent to the Adelaide Botanic Gardens.

facts.fact: The building, designed by Cox Grieve Gillett, uses materials that reflect items used in making wine.
facts.quote: The building designed by Cox Grieve Gillett uses building materials to reflect items used in making wine.

facts.fact: The exterior looks like a section of a wine barrel.
facts.quote: The exterior of the building looks like a section of a wine barrel.

facts.fact: Rows of grapevines outside show seven grape varieties.
facts.quote: Outside the building are rows of grapevines, showing seven different varieties of grapes to curious visitors who normally would not have access to a vineyard to see the differences for themselves.

facts.fact: It opened on 6 October 2001 and has been run by the University of Adelaide since 2003.
facts.quote: It eventually opened on 6 October 2001 after enabling legislation created the concept in the National Wine Centre Act (1997). After a number of problems with funding, management and profitability, the Wine Centre operation was given to the University of Adelaide on 12 September 2003 on a 40-year lease.

facts.fact: The Jubilee Library is the largest public library in Brighton and Hove.
facts.quote: The Jubilee Library is the largest public library in the English city of Brighton and Hove.

facts.fact: It was designed by Bennetts Associates with the Brighton firm LCE Architects.
facts.quote: The scheme architects were Bennetts Associates and Brighton firm LCE Architects (Lomax Cassidy & Edwards); the lead architects of the respective firms have a long association.

facts.fact: It has been called one of England's most energy-efficient buildings, with half the carbon footprint of a comparable traditional public building.
facts.quote: The building has been described as one of the most energy-efficient structures in England –  its carbon footprint is half that of a traditional public building of its comparable size, and natural energy is used throughout.

facts.fact: Glazed blue tiles imitate mathematical tiles, an 18th-century feature common in Brighton but rare elsewhere.
facts.quote: Further to the east, the wing containing staff and conference rooms is faced with glazed blue tiles which imitate mathematical tiles—an 18th-century design element used frequently in Brighton but rarely found elsewhere.

facts.fact: The two-storey forum-style interior has large white concrete columns splayed at the top.
facts.quote: The two-storey forum-style space is interspersed with large white-painted concrete columns splayed at the top.

facts.fact: Daylight enters through the south-facing glass front and is directed by a giant louvre screen.
facts.quote: Natural light comes in through the south-facing glass front and is directed by a giant screen in the form of a louvre which, along with steel and glass passageways, divide the outer glass wall from the interior.

facts.fact: Solar and wind energy heat and cool the building naturally, except in extreme temperatures.
facts.quote: Solar and wind energy are used to heat and cool the building naturally, except during extremes of temperature.

facts.fact: It was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2005.
facts.quote: In 1991 Bennetts Associates were shortlisted for the RIBA Building of the Year Award for Imperium Offices in Reading, and have been shortlisted for its successor, the Stirling Prize, four times: for the Richard Attenborough Centre at the University of Leicester in 1998; for the Jubilee Library in Brighton in 2005; for the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2011; and for the BEAM arts and culture venue in Hertford in 2026.

facts.fact: The River & Rowing Museum stood at Mill Meadows by the Thames in Henley-on-Thames, with galleries on the river, rowing and the town.
facts.quote: The River & Rowing Museum in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire, England, was on a site at Mill Meadows by the River Thames. It had three main themes represented by major permanent galleries, the non-tidal River Thames, the international sport of rowing and the local town of Henley-on-Thames.

facts.fact: It was designed by David Chipperfield and won the Royal Fine Art Commission Building of the Year award in 1999.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the modernist architect Sir David Chipperfield and has won awards for the building itself, including the Royal Fine Art Commission Building of the Year award in 1999.

facts.fact: Queen Elizabeth II opened it in November 1998.
facts.quote: It was officially opened in November 1998 by Queen Elizabeth II.

facts.fact: It was Chipperfield's first major project in Britain.
facts.quote: His first major project in Britain was the River and Rowing Museum in Henley-on-Thames (1989) (see below).

facts.fact: The building blends modernist and traditional forms, inspired by boat sheds and Oxfordshire barns.
facts.quote: The building is a blend of modernist and traditional forms and materials. It was inspired by the form of traditional boat sheds, as well as the traditional barns of Oxfordshire.

facts.fact: It covers 2,300 square metres and is raised on concrete pillars to avoid flooding.
facts.quote: The building occupies a space of 2,300 square metres and is lifted above the ground on concrete pillars to avoid flooding.

facts.fact: Untreated oak planks clad the exterior and parts of the interior, and the roofs and sunscreens are stainless steel.
facts.quote: The exterior and parts of the interior are covered in planks of non-treated oak, matching the local rural architecture. The roofs and sunscreens are of stainless steel.

facts.fact: The museum closed on 21 September 2025, and in March 2026 the Twentieth Century Society applied for the building to be listed.
facts.quote: The museum closed on 21 September 2025. In March 2026 the Twentieth Century Society applied for the building to be listed.

facts.fact: Kirklees Stadium is a multi-purpose stadium in Huddersfield with a capacity of 24,121.
facts.quote: Kirklees Stadium, currently known as the Accu Stadium for sponsorship reasons, is a multi-purpose stadium in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, England. With a capacity of 24,121, it has been the home ground of Huddersfield Town Association Football Club and previously home to Huddersfield Giants Rugby League Club, both of whom moved from Leeds Road in 1994 following a 2-year groundshare arrangement.

facts.fact: It was built by Alfred McAlpine, designed by Populous, and won the RIBA Building of the Year award for 1995.
facts.quote: It was built by Alfred McAlpine, designed by Populous and was awarded the RIBA Building of the Year award for 1995.

facts.fact: The structural engineer Anthony Hunt's list of works includes Kirklees Stadium (1997), with Lobb Partnership as architects.
facts.quote: 1997 Kirklees Stadium, Huddersfield, Yorkshire (architects: Lobb Partnership)

facts.fact: The decision to build was made in August 1992, and it was ready for the 1994–95 season.
facts.quote: The decision to build a new stadium for Huddersfield Town and Huddersfield Giants was made in August 1992. Construction began the following year and it was completed in time for the 1994–95 season, enabling the clubs to move to their new base after 86 years at Leeds Road and 114 years at Fartown respectively, with the Rugby club sharing Leeds Road from 1992 to 1994.

facts.fact: It was built in stages: two side stands at opening, the South Stand in December 1994 and the North Stand in 1996–1998.
facts.quote: When the stadium opened only the two side stands (the Riverside and Kilner Bank stands) were ready. The South Stand was opened in December 1994. Construction on the North (Panasonic) Stand began in 1996 and it was completed in 1998, bringing the overall capacity of the stadium to approximately 24,500.

facts.fact: It hosted Rugby League World Cup matches in 1995, 2000, 2013 and 2021, and the 1999 Rugby World Cup.
facts.quote: The stadium was a venue for the Rugby League World Cup in 1995, 2000, 2013 and 2021, in addition to the 1999 Rugby World Cup.

facts.fact: Kuggen ('the cog') is a building of Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg.
facts.quote: Kuggen (Swedish for 'the (cogwheel) cog') is a building owned by real estate company Chalmersfastigheter as part of Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

facts.fact: It was designed by Wingårdh arkitektkontor and built from October 2010 to March 2011.
facts.quote: It was designed by Wingårdh arkitektkontor. Construction started in October 2010 and completed in March 2011.

facts.fact: The exterior is glazed terracotta in six shades of red and two of green.
facts.quote: The exterior is made of six different shades of red and two shades of green. The building is finished in a glazed terracotta.

facts.fact: It is circular to keep the ratio of skin to floor area low.
facts.quote: ”Kuggen” is circular to minimize the ratio between skin and area.

facts.fact: Each floor adds two bays, so the building grows larger with each storey.
facts.quote: Each floor adds two bays, causing the building to grow larger in size for each additional floor.

facts.fact: A movable sunscreen tracks the sun to shade the top two floors.
facts.quote: A movable sunscreen tracks the sun and contributes to the shade of the two top floors, while nearby buildings cast their shadows on the lower levels.

facts.fact: Triangular windows let daylight follow the ceiling deep inside while keeping glazing to 30% of the facade.
facts.quote: The windows are triangular allowing daylight to follow the ceiling deep into the building while staying at a low ratio (30%) of the elevation surface.

facts.fact: It aims to limit energy use to 60 kWh/m2 a year.
facts.quote: The result is a building that aims to limit energy consumption to 60 kWh/m2 per year—well below what is considered a green building—while providing temperature within individual offices between 22 and 26 degrees Celsius.

facts.fact: The Whitechapel Gallery is a public art gallery on the north side of Whitechapel High Street, in the London Borough of Tower Hamlets.
facts.quote: The Whitechapel Gallery is a public art gallery in Whitechapel on the north side of Whitechapel High Street, in the London Borough of Tower Hamlets.

facts.fact: The original building, designed by Charles Harrison Townsend, opened in 1901 as one of London's first publicly funded galleries for temporary exhibitions.
facts.quote: The original building, designed by Charles Harrison Townsend, opened in 1901 as one of the first publicly funded galleries for temporary exhibitions in London.

facts.fact: The building is a notable example of the British Modern Style.
facts.quote: The building is a notable example of the British Modern Style.

facts.fact: It is one of three strikingly original public buildings in London on which Townsend's reputation rests, designed 1895–1899 and opened in 1901.
facts.quote: Townsend's career was devoted mainly to domestic and small-scale ecclesiastical commissions, but his reputation rests principally on three strikingly original public buildings in London: Bishopsgate Institute (1892–1894); the Whitechapel Art Gallery (1895–1899, opened 1901); and the Horniman Museum (1898–1901).

facts.fact: The gallery showed Picasso's Guernica in 1938, in a touring exhibition organised by Roland Penrose to protest against the Spanish Civil War.
facts.quote: The gallery exhibited Pablo Picasso's Guernica in 1938 as part of a touring exhibition organised by Roland Penrose to protest against the Spanish Civil War.

facts.fact: Shows held here include This is Tomorrow in 1956, Mark Rothko's first UK exhibition in 1961 and The New Generation in 1964.
facts.quote: Several significant exhibitions were held at the Whitechapel Gallery including This is Tomorrow in 1956, the first UK exhibition by Mark Rothko in 1961, and in 1964, The New Generation show which featured John Hoyland, Bridget Riley, David Hockney and Patrick Caulfield among others.

facts.fact: In 2009 the gallery roughly doubled in size by taking in the former Passmore Edwards library building next door.
facts.quote: In 2009 the gallery approximately doubled in size by incorporating the adjacent former Passmore Edwards library building.

facts.fact: The expansion nearly tripled the exhibition space and lets the gallery stay open all year round.
facts.quote: The expansion, which doubled the gallery's physical size and nearly tripled its available exhibition space, now allows the Whitechapel Gallery to remain open to the public all year round.

facts.fact: Mumok, the Museum moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig Wien, is a museum of modern art in the MuseumsQuartier in Vienna.
facts.quote: Mumok, officially the Museum moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig Wien, (transl. Museum of modern art, Ludwig Foundation, Vienna) is a museum in the Museumsquartier in Vienna, Austria.

facts.fact: Since 2001 the museum has been housed in a stone-clad building designed by the Austrian architects Ortner & Ortner.
facts.quote: Since 2001, the museum has been housed in a stone-clad building designed by Austrian architects Ortner & Ortner.

facts.fact: The cubic building is clad in basalt lava and provides 4,800 m² of exhibition space for some 10,000 works of modern and contemporary art.
facts.quote: This cubic building clad in basalt lava was built by architects Ortner & Ortner, and provides 4,800 m2 of exhibition space for monographic or thematic exhibitions and alternating presentations of the museum's own collection, which now contain some 10,000 works of modernist and contemporary art.

facts.fact: The museum reopened in its new home in the MuseumsQuartier on 15 September 2001.
facts.quote: On 15 September 2001, the Museum moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig Wien was reopened in the MuseumsQuartier in Vienna's historical center.

facts.fact: The MuseumsQuartier sets historic Baroque buildings beside contemporary museum architecture on the site of the former imperial court stables.
facts.quote: Opened in 2001 on the site of the former imperial court stables, it combines historic Baroque buildings with contemporary museum architecture.

facts.fact: The contrast between the historic enclosure and the modern volumes of the Leopold Museum and MUMOK is a defining feature of the complex.
facts.quote: The contrast between the historic enclosure and the modern volumes of the Leopold Museum and MUMOK is a defining feature of the complex.

facts.fact: The new buildings were set into the old stable complex to form a sequence of courtyards, passages and cultural venues.
facts.quote: The new buildings were inserted into the large former stable complex, creating a sequence of courtyards, passages and cultural venues rather than a single museum building.

facts.fact: The museum is known for its large collection of art related to Viennese Actionism.
facts.quote: The Mumok regularly organizes special exhibitions and is known for its large collection of art related to Viennese Actionism.

facts.fact: The Zwinger is a palace complex with gardens in Dresden, designed by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann and one of the most important Baroque buildings in Germany.
facts.quote: The Zwinger (German: Dresdner Zwinger, IPA: [ˈdʁeːzdnɐ ˈt͡svɪŋɐ]) is a palatial complex with gardens in Dresden, Germany. Designed by architect Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann, it is one of the most important buildings of the Baroque period in Germany.

facts.fact: It was built as an orangery and garden and as a showpiece festival area.
facts.quote: The Zwinger was built in 1709 as an orangery and garden as well as a representative festival area.

facts.fact: Its richly decorated pavilions and galleries lined with balustrades, figures and vases show the splendour of Augustus the Strong's reign.
facts.quote: Its richly decorated pavilions and the galleries lined with balustrades, figures and vases testify to the splendor during the reign of Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony and elected King of Poland.

facts.fact: Pöppelmann designed it and it was built in stages from 1710 to 1728, with sculpture by Balthasar Permoser.
facts.quote: The Zwinger was designed by Pöppelmann and constructed in stages from 1710 to 1728. Sculpture was provided by Balthasar Permoser.

facts.fact: The Zwinger was planned as the forecourt of a new castle reaching to the Elbe, so it was left open on the river side.
facts.quote: In the original conception of the elector, the Zwinger was the forecourt of a new castle that would take up the area between it and the Elbe; therefore, the Zwinger remained undeveloped on the Elbe side (provisionally closed with a wall).

facts.fact: The Kronentor, the crown gate, was finished in 1714 and takes the shape of the Polish crown.
facts.quote: The Kronentor was built and finished in 1714 as an add-on to the Zwinger. The Kronentor is also a national monument, built with dark wood and gold in the shape of the Polish crown, further cementing Augustus II the Strong's claim to the Polish throne.

facts.fact: In 1847–1855 Gottfried Semper closed the open side with the gallery wing later named the Semper Gallery.
facts.quote: Later the plans were changed to a smaller scale, and in 1847–1855 the area was closed by the construction of the gallery wing now separating the Zwinger from the Theatre Square. The architect of this building, later named Semper Gallery, was Gottfried Semper.

facts.fact: Mostly destroyed in the bombing of February 1945, the Zwinger had largely been restored to its pre-war state by 1963.
facts.quote: The building was mostly destroyed by the carpet bombing raids of 13–15 February 1945. The art collection had been previously evacuated, however. Reconstruction, supported by the Soviet military administration, began in 1945; parts of the restored complex were opened to the public in 1951. By 1963 the Zwinger had largely been restored to its pre-war state.

facts.fact: Balthasar Neumann was the principal architect of the Residence, a palace commissioned by the Prince-Bishop of Würzburg and his brother in 1720 and completed in 1744.
facts.quote: Balthasar Neumann, court architect of the Bishop of Würzburg, was the principal architect of the Residence, which was commissioned by the Prince-Bishop of Würzburg Johann Philipp Franz von Schönborn and his brother Friedrich Carl von Schönborn in 1720, and completed in 1744.

facts.fact: Its interiors considered masterworks include the grand staircase, the chapel and the Imperial Hall.
facts.quote: Interiors considered masterworks of Baroque/Rococo or Neoclassical architecture and art include the grand staircase, the chapel, and the Imperial Hall.

facts.fact: The palace stands on a base of 92 × 167 metres: a central wing with north and south blocks, each with two interior courts.
facts.quote: The Residence was constructed on a base plate of 92 × 167 meters. The main structure consists of a central wing with two side wings, the north and south blocks, each with two interior courts.

facts.fact: The staircase vault spans an area of 18 by 32 metres without pillars.
facts.quote: The staircase of the Würzburg Residence spans its vault, an area of 18 by 32 meters (59 ft × 105 ft), without pillars.

facts.fact: The stair first leads towards a blank wall, then splits and doubles back, so the host on the upper landing saw his visitors first.
facts.quote: The lowest part of the stair leads away from the reception hall, towards a blank wall and then splits into two stairs which double back. Thus, the host on the upper landing was able to see his visitors first who initially walked away from him.

facts.fact: The staircase is vaulted by the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world, about 580 m², painted in 1752–53 by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo and his sons.
facts.quote: The enormous staircase is vaulted by the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world (approx. 580 m2), painted between 1752 and 1753 by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo as well as his sons − especially Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo − and other helpers.

facts.fact: Neumann's stone vaults withstood the collapse of the burning attic.
facts.quote: Neumann's stone vaults withstood the collapse of the burning attic.

facts.fact: The Residence has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981 for its outstanding Baroque art, design and architecture.
facts.quote: Since 1981, the Residence has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site in recognition of its outstanding Baroque art, design, and architecture.

facts.fact: The Siemensstadt Settlement, also called the Ringsiedlung, is a nonprofit housing estate in Berlin's Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf district.
facts.quote: The Siemensstadt Settlement (German: Großsiedlung Siemensstadt; also known as Ring Settlement or Ringsiedlung) is a nonprofit residential community in the Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf district of Berlin.

facts.fact: It is one of six Modernist Housing Estates in Berlin listed by UNESCO in 2008 for their modernist architecture and their part in Weimar-era housing reform.
facts.quote: It is one of the six Modernist Housing Estates in Berlin recognized in July 2008 by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site because of their outstanding modernist architecture and contribution to the progressive housing reform movement during the Weimar Republic.

facts.fact: It was built between 1929 and 1931 to a master plan by Hans Scharoun.
facts.quote: It was built between 1929 and 1931, under the overall master plan of German architect Hans Scharoun.

facts.fact: Six Weimar-era architects took part: Scharoun, Fred Forbát, Otto Bartning, Walter Gropius, Paul Rudolph Henning and Hugo Häring.
facts.quote: Six prominent Weimar-era architects took part: Hans Scharoun, Fred Forbát, Otto Bartning, Walter Gropius, Paul Rudolph Henning, and Hugo Häring.

facts.fact: The nickname Ringsiedlung comes from some of these architects' ties to the Der Ring collective.
facts.quote: The nickname Ringsiedlung came from the association of some of these architects with Der Ring collective.

facts.fact: The open spaces were designed by the modernist landscape architect Leberecht Migge.
facts.quote: The open spaces were designed by the German modernist landscape architect Leberecht Migge.

facts.fact: A private housing cooperative built it as worker housing for Siemens' nearby electrical factory.
facts.quote: Unlike the other significant public housing projects of the time, which were produced under government cooperative Gehag sponsorship, the Siemensstadt was constructed by a private housing cooperative as worker housing for Siemens' nearby electrical factory, which employed 60,000 workers.

facts.fact: The estate marked the point where Berlin's planners moved from low-rise garden-city housing to denser multi-storey apartment blocks.
facts.quote: The shape of the settlement marked a turning point in urban thinking, the point at which Berlin's city planner Martin Wagner abandoned a low-rise, garden city-style project with individual gardens, in favor of much denser multi-story apartment blocks.

facts.fact: The Karlskirche is a Baroque church on Karlsplatz in Vienna, dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo.
facts.quote: The Karlskirche (English: Charles Church) is a Baroque church in the Karlsplatz in Vienna, Austria. The church is dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation.

facts.fact: In 1713, a year after Vienna's last major plague, Emperor Charles VI pledged to build a church to Charles Borromeo, revered as a healer of plague sufferers.
facts.quote: In 1713, one year after the last major plague epidemic in Vienna, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, pledged to build a church dedicated to his namesake patron saint, Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer for plague sufferers.

facts.fact: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach won the competition, beating Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt.
facts.quote: An architectural competition was announced, in which Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach won over competitors including Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt.

facts.fact: After his death in 1723, his son Joseph Emanuel Fischer von Erlach completed the church in 1737, changing the original plans.
facts.quote: After J.B. Fischer's death in 1723, his son, Joseph Emanuel Fischer von Erlach, completed the construction in 1737 with modifications to the original plans.

facts.fact: The central façade is a Greek temple portico, flanked by two columns inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome.
facts.quote: The façade in the centre, which leads to the porch, corresponds to a Greek temple portico. The two flanking columns, crafted by Lorenzo Mattielli, were inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome.

facts.fact: Two tower pavilions show the influence of Roman Baroque, and a dome rises above a high drum.
facts.quote: Next to those, two tower pavilions extend out and show the influence of the Roman baroque (Bernini and Borromini). Above the entrance, a dome rises up above a high drum, which the younger J.E. Fischer shortened and partly altered.

facts.fact: Fischer aimed to bring together the main ideas of the great churches of Western architecture, from the Temple of Solomon and Hagia Sophia to the Pantheon and St Peter's.
facts.quote: In this structure, completed by his son Joseph Emanuel, Fischer's ambition was to harmonize the principal elements and ideas that underlie the most significant churches in the history of Western architecture: the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem, Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the Pantheon and Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, the Dome des Invalides in Paris and Saint Paul's Cathedral in London.

facts.fact: The church is considered Fischer's greatest work.
facts.quote: Next to the structures at Schönbrunn Palace, which maintain this form but are more fragmented, the church is considered Fischer's greatest work.

facts.fact: The Wieskirche is a Roman Catholic oval Rococo pilgrimage church, designed in the late 1740s and completed in 1754.
facts.quote: The Pilgrimage Church of Wies (officially: Wallfahrtskirche zum Gegeißelten Heiland auf der Wies ("Pilgrimage Church of the Scourged Savior on the Meadow"); abbr. Wieskirche ("Meadow Church")) is a Roman Catholic oval Rococo church, designed in the late 1740s and completed in 1754.

facts.fact: It is the major work of the brothers Johann Baptist and Dominikus Zimmermann.
facts.quote: It is the major work of the brothers Johann Baptist and Dominikus Zimmermann, the latter of whom lived nearby for the last eleven years of his life.

facts.fact: A small chapel built in 1740 to house the revered statue soon proved too small for the pilgrims, so Steingaden Abbey commissioned a separate shrine.
facts.quote: In 1740, a small chapel was built to house the statue but it was soon realized that the building would be too small for the number of pilgrims it attracted, and so Steingaden Abbey decided to commission a separate shrine.

facts.fact: It was built between 1745 and 1754 and decorated with frescoes and stuccowork in the Wessobrunner School tradition.
facts.quote: Construction took place between 1745 and 1754, and the interior was decorated with frescoes and with stuccowork in the tradition of the Wessobrunner School.

facts.fact: The church has an oval plan with a semi-circular narthex; inside, twin columns support an elaborate cornice, with a long, deep choir.
facts.quote: The Wieskirche has an oval plan, with a semi-circular narthex. Inside, twin columns in front of the walls support the elaborate cornice, with elaborate stucco decorations (painted by J. B. Zimmermann) and a long, deep choir.

facts.fact: The ceilings are painted in trompe-l'œil and seem to open up to an iridescent sky.
facts.quote: The ceilings are painted in a trompe-l'œil style, appearing to open up to an iridescent sky.

facts.fact: The church was extensively restored between 1985 and 1991.
facts.quote: The church underwent extensive restoration between 1985 and 1991.

facts.fact: It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 for its outstanding Rococo architecture.
facts.quote: Because of its outstanding Rococo architecture, the Wieskirche was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983.

facts.fact: The Sprinkenhof is a nine-storey office building built between 1927 and 1943 in Hamburg's Kontorhaus District.
facts.quote: The Sprinkenhof is a nine-storey office building built between 1927 and 1943 in Hamburg's Kontorhaus District.

facts.fact: The Chilehaus stands directly to its northeast, across the main road.
facts.quote: The Chilehaus is located directly to the northeast, separated only by the main road.

facts.fact: The architects Fritz Höger and Hans and Oskar Gerson planned and built it together; planning began in 1925.
facts.quote: The architects Fritz Höger and Hans and Oskar Gerson worked together on the planning and execution of the building. Planning began in 1925.

facts.fact: The Gersons took inspiration from the Doge's Palace in Venice and the Casa de las Conchas in Salamanca.
facts.quote: The Gersons were inspired by both the Doge's Palace in Venice and the Casa de las Conchas in Salamanca.

facts.fact: It has a reinforced-concrete skeleton and is an example of Brick Expressionism; when built it was Europe's largest office building.
facts.quote: The Sprinkenhof was built in skeleton construction made from reinforced concrete and is another example of Brick Expressionism. At the time of its construction it was Europe's largest office building.

facts.fact: Rhombic clinker patterns on the facade underline the block character, with further clinker and terracotta decoration.
facts.quote: The facade was decorated with rhombic clinker patterns to underline the block character. In addition, the facade was decorated with clinker and terracotta.

facts.fact: Hamburg's first underground car park was built in its basement.
facts.quote: Hamburg's first underground car park was built in the basement of the Sprinkenhof.

facts.fact: As part of the Kontorhaus District, it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.
facts.quote: As part of Kontorhaus District, the Sprinkenhof was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

facts.fact: Yenidze is a former cigarette factory in Dresden, built between 1907 and 1909 and now used as offices.
facts.quote: Yenidze is a former cigarette factory building in Dresden, Saxony, Germany built between 1907 and 1909. Today it is used as an office building.

facts.fact: Its Moorish Revival exterior borrows design elements from mosques and the Alhambra in Spain.
facts.quote: It is notable for its Moorish Revival exterior design which borrows design elements from mosques and the Alhambra in Spain.

facts.fact: The 'Oriental' style recalled the origins of the tobacco the firm processed and worked as advertising.
facts.quote: The "Oriental" style of architecture recalled the exotic origins of the Oriental tobaccos it processed and functioned as advertising for the firm.

facts.fact: The architect Martin Hammitzsch designed the building in 1907.
facts.quote: The architect Martin Hammitzsch (the second husband of Angela Hitler) designed the building in 1907.

facts.fact: It has 600 windows of various styles and a dome 20 metres high.
facts.quote: It has 600 windows of various styles; the dome is 20 metres (66 ft) high.

facts.fact: Tiles are used heavily for decoration, in complex colour patterns and unusual three-dimensional forms.
facts.quote: It makes great use of tiles for decoration: both complex colour patterns and unusual three-dimensional forms.

facts.fact: Its large coloured dome chimneys resemble minarets.
facts.quote: It has large, colored dome chimneys which resemble minarets.

facts.fact: It escaped the February 1945 bombing of Dresden relatively unharmed, while most surrounding buildings were destroyed.
facts.quote: In the carpet bombing of Dresden on 14/15 February 1945 most of the surrounding buildings were obliterated, but Yenidze escaped relatively unharmed, other than some loss of coloured glass in the dome.

facts.fact: Universum Bremen is a science museum in Bremen where visitors can interact with most of its roughly 250 exhibits.
facts.quote: The Universum Bremen is a science museum in Bremen, Germany. Visitors are encouraged to interact with most of the approximately 250 exhibits.

facts.fact: It opened in September 2000 near the University of Bremen.
facts.quote: The Universum Bremen opened in September 2000 near to the University of Bremen, Germany.

facts.fact: Its exhibition covers over 4,000 m², on three themes: mankind, earth and the cosmos.
facts.quote: Covering over 4,000 m2 the exhibition contains exhibits related to one of the three topics: mankind, earth and the cosmos.

facts.fact: The building, clad in 40,000 stainless steel scales, resembles a mixture of a whale and a mussel; it was designed by the Bremen architect Thomas Klumpp.
facts.quote: The science center building, with its 40,000 stainless steel scales, resembles a mixture between a whale and mussel. It was designed by the Bremen architect Thomas Klumpp.

facts.fact: In 2007 a cubic, rust-red building, the SchauBox by Haslob Kruse and Partner, was added in contrast to the curved metallic original.
facts.quote: In contrast to the curved metallic older building, the SchauBox, developed by Haslob Kruse and Partner, is cubic with a rust-red exterior.

facts.fact: The Goetz Collection is a private collection of contemporary art in Munich, opened in 1992.
facts.quote: The Goetz Collection (Sammlung Goetz) is a private collection of contemporary art in Munich, Germany. It opened in 1992.

facts.fact: Its owner, the former gallery dealer Ingvild Goetz, shows the collection in themed exhibitions in a purpose-built museum.
facts.quote: The collection is owned and continually being enlarged by the former gallery dealer Ingvild Goetz, who presents the collection to the public in a series of themed exhibitions in a purpose built museum.

facts.fact: Exhibitions and video and film programmes are held on the lower level of the building.
facts.quote: Sammlung Goetz organizes exhibitions along with video and film programmes on the lower level of the building.

facts.fact: The building was designed by the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the Swiss architectural firm Herzog & de Meuron.

facts.fact: The Goetz Collection building of 1992 used glass cladding to diffuse natural light, and helped build the firm's international reputation in the 1990s.
facts.quote: Their international reputation grew in the 1990s with projects like the Goetz Collection in Munich (1992), which featured glass cladding to diffuse natural light, and the Dominus Winery in Napa Valley (1997), notable for its gabion walls of local stones that integrate the structure with its surroundings.

facts.fact: St. Jakob-Park is a sports stadium in Basel, the largest football venue in Switzerland and home to FC Basel.
facts.quote: St. Jakob-Park (Swiss Standard German: [zaŋkt ˈjaːkɔb ˌpark] ) is a Swiss sports stadium in Basel. It is the largest football venue in Switzerland and home to FC Basel.

facts.fact: Construction began on 13 December 1998, replacing the former St. Jakob Stadium, and the reopening game was played on 15 March 2001.
facts.quote: St. Jakob Park is a fairly modern stadium; construction started on 13 December 1998, replacing the former St. Jakob Stadium. The re-opening game took place on 15 March 2001.

facts.fact: The stadium is divided into four main blocks, one on each side, plus an upper balcony added later.
facts.quote: The stadium is divided into four main blocks, A, B, C and D, each block covering one side of the stadium, and block G, consisting of the upper balcony added later.

facts.fact: Inside are 32 shops on three floors and two restaurants.
facts.quote: Within the stadium, there are 32 shops on three different floors, as well as two restaurants (the "Restaurant UNO" and "Hattrick Sports Bar").

facts.fact: Capacity was raised to 42,500 for Euro 2008 and later cut to 38,512 for league matches and 37,500 for international matches.
facts.quote: The capacity was increased to 42,500 for Euro 2008, which was hosted by Austria and Switzerland. After the tournament, a number of seats were removed, thus creating more space between them. The capacity was therefore reduced to 38,512 for Swiss Super League matches or 37,500 seats for international matches The maximum capacity for concerts is 40,000.

facts.fact: The stadium cost around CHF 220 million to build.
facts.quote: The stadium cost around CHF 220 million to build (US$132 million, €143 million in March 2001).

facts.fact: It is named after the village of St. Jakob an der Birs, which stood on the site.
facts.quote: The stadium is named after the village of St. Jakob an der Birs, which stood on the site.

facts.fact: Hangar-7 is an events venue, gallery and museum beside Salzburg Airport, built by Red Bull to bring together art, aviation and food.
facts.quote: Hangar-7 is an events venue, gallery and museum space adjacent to Salzburg Airport in Austria. It was built by Red Bull GmbH to bring together arts, aviation and the culinary arts.

facts.fact: It houses the Michelin-starred restaurant Ikarus alongside rotating exhibitions of historic aircraft, helicopters and Formula One cars.
facts.quote: The building hosts the Michelin-starred restaurant Ikarus, two bars and a lounge alongside a collection of historical airplanes, helicopters, Formula One racing cars, and more in rotating exhibitions.

facts.fact: Hangar-7 was designed by Volkmar Burgstaller; the airfoil-shaped building uses 1,200 tons of steel and 75,000 sq ft of glass.
facts.quote: Hangar 7 was designed by Volkmar Burgstaller. The building is airfoil shaped, constructed of 1,200 tons of steel and 75,000 sqft of glass surface.

facts.fact: The steel-and-glass dome was engineered and built by the Austrian firm Waagner-Biro and completed in 2003.
facts.quote: The steel-and-glass dome-shaped structure was engineered and built by Austrian specialists Waagner-Biro and completed in 2003.

facts.fact: It was designed for the Flying Bulls aircraft fleet, with a 40 m wide door so their largest plane, a Douglas DC-6B, fits inside.
facts.quote: The building was specifically designed to accommodate the fleet of The Flying Bulls. The building's 40m wide door was developed to allow them to fit their largest plane, a Douglas DC-6B, inside.

facts.fact: Hangar-7 is counted among Salzburg's examples of blob architecture.
facts.quote: Other examples of contemporary architecture lie outside the old town: the Faculty of Science building (Universität Salzburg – Architecture Willhelm Holzbauer) built on the edge of free green space, the blob architecture of Red Bull Hangar-7 (Architecture: Volkmar Burgstaller) at Salzburg Airport, home to Dietrich Mateschitz's Flying Bulls and the Europark Shopping Centre.

facts.fact: The Conference Pavilion is a building on the Vitra Campus in Weil am Rhein, designed by Tadao Ando and built in 1993 as his first building outside Japan.
facts.quote: The Conference Pavilion is a building on the Vitra Campus in Weil am Rhein, Germany. It was designed by Tadao Ando and built in 1993, marking the Japanese architect's first building outside of Japan.

facts.fact: It holds a set of conference rooms, with paths outside described as reminiscent of Japanese monasteries.
facts.quote: Designed by Ando, the building was completed in 1993 and provides a set of conference rooms within, as well as various paths outside "reminiscent of Japanese monasteries."

facts.fact: Ando's minimalism of gridded concrete and holes for light defines the building, which is surrounded by cherry trees.
facts.quote: His characteristic minimalism, of gridded concrete and holes for light, defines the style of the building, which is surrounded by cherry trees.

facts.fact: The Walter Gropius House is a nine-floor block of 66 apartments on Händelallee in Berlin's Hansaviertel, bordering the Tiergarten park.
facts.quote: The Walter Gropius House (also known as Gropiushaus) is a residential building with nine floors and 66 apartments at the Händelallee 1-9 in Berlin Hansaviertel, bordering its central Grosser Tiergarten park.

facts.fact: It was designed by Walter Gropius and The Architects' Collaborative with Wils Ebert for the first International Building Exhibition, Interbau, in 1957.
facts.quote: It was designed by Walter Gropius / The Architects' Collaborative - TAC (Cambridge, Massachusetts, US) in collaboration with Wils Ebert, Berlin, on the occasion of the first International Building Exhibition ("Interbau"), in 1957.

facts.fact: It is regarded as an important modernist landmark and was listed as a monument in 1980.
facts.quote: It is regarded as an important modernist landmark and was declared listed monument in 1980.

facts.fact: Its characteristic features are a concave form, a textured facade and distinctive narrow ends.
facts.quote: Characteristic features of the Walter Gropius house are its concave structure, textured facade and distinctive narrow sides.

facts.fact: Balconies grouped in fours form a checkerboard pattern with the windows and concrete plaster walls.
facts.quote: They differ mainly in the position of the balconies, which are grouped into groups of four, thus creating a distinctive "checkerboard pattern" alternating with the window areas and concrete plaster walls.

facts.fact: Instead of blank end walls, Gropius turned four apartments at each end to face east or west.
facts.quote: A further special feature is the design of the narrow sides: whereas linear block (Zeilenbau) buildings typically feature windowless narrow sides, Gropius has rotated four apartments at both ends of the building in the east and / or west direction.

facts.fact: The apartment plans are based on Gropius's contribution to the Siemensstadt estate of 1929–30.
facts.quote: The ground plans of the apartments are based on Gropius's contribution to the Siemensstadt settlement of 1929-30.

facts.fact: Because the house is a concrete skeleton with few load-bearing walls, the apartments could have open-plan kitchen and living areas.
facts.quote: Since the house is built as a concrete skeleton, the apartments have only a few load-bearing walls, so that open-plan kitchen/living-areas can be created.

facts.fact: The University Library Freiburg is the academic and research library of the University of Freiburg, also open to the public.
facts.quote: The University Library Freiburg (German: Universitätsbibliothek Freiburg, UB) is the library of the University of Freiburg. As an academic and research library, it caters to students and staff of the University of Freiburg, the University of Education Freiburg, the Catholic University of Applied Sciences Freiburg, and the Protestant University of Applied Sciences Freiburg. The library is open to interested members of the public as well.

facts.fact: An architectural competition in early 2006 to rebuild the library was won by Degelo Architekten of Basel.
facts.quote: In early 2006, the reconstruction was initiated by an architectural design competition. The winner was Degelo Architekten, an architecture firm from Basel.

facts.fact: After the shell was completed in April 2013, work began on a 7,300 m² facade of glass and matted dark chrome steel.
facts.quote: The shell was completed in April 2013. In the same month, interior construction began, as well as the installation of a 7,300 m2 facade of glass and matted, dark chrome steel.

facts.fact: The central idea of the design was workspaces around the outside of each floor, with the books stored in the centre.
facts.quote: The central concept behind the building's design was to have workspaces around the exterior of each floor with books stored in the center.

facts.fact: On the upper floors the two sections of each floor are divided by a glass wall, so they connect only through the ground floor.
facts.quote: You can only pass from one side to the next via the ground floor, as the two sections on each floor above that one are divided by a glass wall.

facts.fact: The new building is 20% smaller in volume than the old one and offers 1,700 workspaces.
facts.quote: The new building is 20% smaller in volume than the previous building; however, it offers a net floor area that is 30,600 m2 greater than the previous building and a total of 1,700 workspaces.

facts.fact: Reflections from the glass front's southeastern corner dazzle traffic when the sun is low, so canvas blinds cover it in spring and autumn.
facts.quote: Further difficulties with the building include the fact that traffic participants are blinded by the reflections on the southeastern corner of the glass front when the sun is low in spring and fall. For this reason, canvas blinds are used to cover it during these times.

facts.fact: The library was officially handed over to the university on 12 October 2015; construction cost 53 million euros in total.
facts.quote: On 12 October 2015, the library was officially handed over to the university in the presence of two federal ministers. Construction in total then cost 53 million euros.

facts.fact: Neues Museum Nürnberg is a museum for modern and contemporary art and design in Nuremberg.
facts.quote: Neues Museum Nürnberg (NMN) is a museum for modern and contemporary art and design in Nuremberg.

facts.fact: In 1990 the Bavarian government decided to build a museum for 20th-century art.
facts.quote: In 1990 the Bavarian government decided to build a 20th-century museum.

facts.fact: The building was designed by the architect Volker Staab.
facts.quote: The building in which the museum is located was designed by the architect Volker Staab.

facts.fact: Construction ran from 11 September 1996 to October 1999, and the museum officially opened on 15 April 2000.
facts.quote: Construction started on 11 September 1996 and ended in October 1999. The official opening was on 15. April 2000.

facts.fact: It shows contemporary art and design from the 1950s onwards on 3,000 m².
facts.quote: On 3000 sq/m contemporary art as well as art and design dating back to the 1950s is being shown.

facts.fact: In 2001 the museum won the Deutscher Natursteinpreis and a special recognition of the Deutscher Städtebaupreis.
facts.quote: 2001: Deutscher Natursteinpreis for New Museum Nuremberg 2001: Special recognition of the Deutscher Städtebaupreis for New Museum Nuremberg

facts.fact: Mossehaus is an office building on Schützenstraße in Berlin, renovated with a new corner by Erich Mendelsohn between 1921 and 1923.
facts.quote: Mossehaus is an office building on 18–25 Schützenstraße in Berlin, renovated and with a corner designed by Erich Mendelsohn between 1921 and 1923.

facts.fact: It housed the printing press and offices of Rudolf Mosse's newspapers, such as the liberal Berliner Tageblatt.
facts.quote: The original Mosse building housed the printing press and offices of the newspapers owned by Rudolf Mosse, mainly liberal newspapers such as the Berliner Tageblatt.

facts.fact: On the strength of his Einstein Tower, Mendelsohn was hired in 1921 to add storeys and a new entrance to the building.
facts.quote: In 1921, on the strength of his Einstein Tower, Mendelsohn was hired to add extra storeys and a new entrance to the building.

facts.fact: The new frontage made prominent use of aluminium and modern typography, and the new upper floors were built of reinforced concrete.
facts.quote: The new frontage made prominent use of aluminum and modern typography, and the new upper floors were made from ferro-concrete.

facts.fact: Strips and sculpted elements in the windows gave it a dynamic form, contrasting with the older Wilhelmine style.
facts.quote: The use of strips and sculpted elements in the fenestration gave it a dynamic, futuristic form, emphasised by the contrast with the earlier Wilhelmine style.

facts.fact: It was one of the first streamlined buildings and a great influence on Streamline Moderne.
facts.quote: It was one of the first examples of a streamlined building, and hence a great influence on Streamline Moderne.

facts.fact: Richard Neutra was Mendelsohn's partner on the Mossehaus and designed its interiors.
facts.quote: The effect on American architecture is perhaps unsurprising, as Mendelsohn's partner on the Mossehaus and the designer of the interiors was Richard Neutra.

facts.fact: The building was restored to its original splendour in the 1990s.
facts.quote: The building was restored to its original splendor in the 1990s.

facts.fact: The Olympiastadion is a sports stadium at Olympiapark Berlin, designed by Werner March for the 1936 Summer Olympics.
facts.quote: Olympiastadion (German pronunciation: [oˈlʏmpi̯aˌʃtaːdi̯ɔn] ), also known in English as the Berlin Olympic Stadium or simply the Olympic Stadium, is a sports stadium at Olympiapark Berlin in Berlin, Germany. It was originally designed by Werner March for the 1936 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: The Nazi government commissioned the complex, including the stadium, and built it between 1934 and 1936 with state funds.
facts.quote: The complex, including the Olympiastadion, was commissioned by the Nazi government and constructed between 1934 and 1936 using state funds.

facts.fact: March built the stadium on the foundation of the earlier Deutsches Stadion, with the lower half sunk 12 metres below ground.
facts.quote: Werner March built the new Olympiastadion on the foundation of the original Deutsches Stadion, once again with the lower half of the structure recessed 12 metres (40 feet) below ground level.

facts.fact: The Bell Tower was rebuilt in 1960–1962, again by Werner March, following the original blueprints.
facts.quote: A reconstruction of the tower was built between 1960 and 1962, once again by the architect Werner March, following the original blueprints.

facts.fact: In the renovation the playing field was lowered by 2.65 metres to give football a more intimate atmosphere.
facts.quote: With the intention of creating a more intimate atmosphere for football games, the playing field was lowered by 2.65 metres (8.7 ft).

facts.fact: The roof rises 68 metres over the seats and is made of transparent panels that let in daylight.
facts.quote: The roof rises 68 metres (223 ft) over the seats and is made up of transparent panels that allow sunlight to stream in during the day.

facts.fact: The western end, at the Marathon Arch, is left open so spectators can see the Bell Tower.
facts.quote: The western portion (on the Marathon Arch) is open to reveal the Bell Tower to the spectators.

facts.fact: Its value as a historic monument was considered in the renovation, especially the preservation of the natural stone blocks.
facts.quote: The conservation factor of the Olympiastadion as a historical monument was also considered, especially with respect to the preservation of the natural stone blocks.

facts.fact: The Neue Wache is a listed building on Unter den Linden in Berlin, built 1816–1818 to plans by Karl Friedrich Schinkel as a guardhouse for the Royal Palace and a memorial to the Liberation Wars.
facts.quote: The Neue Wache (lit. 'New Watchhouse') is a listed building on Unter den Linden boulevard in the historic centre of Berlin, Germany. Erected from 1816 to 1818 according to plans by Karl Friedrich Schinkel as a guardhouse for the Royal Palace and a memorial to the Liberation Wars, it is considered a major work of Prussian Neoclassical architecture.

facts.fact: It was Schinkel's first major commission in Berlin.
facts.quote: He commissioned Schinkel, the leading exponent of Neoclassical architecture, to design the building: this was Schinkel's first major commission in Berlin.

facts.fact: The plain building has four massive corner blocks and a portico of baseless Doric columns in the original Greek form.
facts.quote: Located between the Zeughaus and the Humboldt University, the plain building is characterised by four massive corner risalits and a portico of Doric columns, of the original Greek form, without bases.

facts.fact: Schinkel based the plan on a Roman castrum, with four sturdy corner towers and an inner courtyard.
facts.quote: Schinkel wrote of his design: "The plan of this completely exposed building, free on all sides, is approximately the shape of a Roman castrum, thus the four sturdier corner towers and the inner courtyard."

facts.fact: In 1931 Heinrich Tessenow turned the interior into a war memorial hall around a black granite block, under an oculus.
facts.quote: In 1931 the architect Heinrich Tessenow was commissioned by the Free State of Prussia to redesign the building as a war memorial to commemorate those who died in the Great War. Tessenow converted the interior into a memorial hall centered around a black granite block with an oak wreath designed by the sculptor Ludwig Gies, situated under an oculus (circular skylight).

facts.fact: Since 1993 it has been the Central Memorial of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Victims of War and Tyranny.
facts.quote: Following German Reunification, the site has also been, since 1993, the Central Memorial of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Victims of War and Tyranny.

facts.fact: An enlarged version of Käthe Kollwitz's Mother with her Dead Son sits directly under the oculus, open to rain, snow and cold.
facts.quote: At the personal suggestion of the Federal Chancellor of Germany Helmut Kohl, the East German memorial piece was removed and replaced by an enlarged version of Käthe Kollwitz's sculpture Mother with her Dead Son. The pietà-style sculpture is directly placed under the oculus, and so is exposed to the rain, snow and cold of the Berlin climate, symbolizing the suffering of civilians during and after both World Wars.

facts.fact: The Rheinturm is a 240.5-metre concrete telecommunications tower in Düsseldorf, built from 1979 to 1981.
facts.quote: The Rheinturm (pronounced [ˈʁaɪntʊʁm]; 'Rhine Tower') is a 240.5-metre-high (789 ft) concrete telecommunications tower in Düsseldorf, capital of the federal state (Bundesland) of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Construction commenced in 1979 and finished in 1981.

facts.fact: The Rheinturm (1979–1981) is listed among Harald Deilmann's projects.
facts.quote: Miscellaneous: 1979–1981: Rheinturm Düsseldorf

facts.fact: It houses a revolving restaurant and an observation deck at 168 metres, and is the tallest building in Düsseldorf.
facts.quote: It stands 172.5 metres (564ft) tall and houses a revolving restaurant and an observation deck at a height of 168 metres (551ft). It is the tallest building in Düsseldorf.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 1 December 1981, contains 7,500 m³ of concrete and weighs 22,500 tons.
facts.quote: The Rheinturm was inaugurated on 1 December 1981. It contains 7,500 cubic metres of concrete and weighs 22,500 tons.

facts.fact: A light sculpture on the shaft by Horst H. Baumann, the Lichtzeitpegel, works as a clock.
facts.quote: As a special attraction, a light sculpture on its shaft works as a clock. This sculpture was designed by Horst H. Baumann and is called Lichtzeitpegel (light time level).

facts.fact: The light sculpture is the largest digital clock in the world.
facts.quote: The light sculpture on the Rheinturm is the largest digital clock in the world.

facts.fact: The Performing Arts Centre in Esbjerg is among the works Jan Utzon, son of Jørn Utzon, completed on his own.
facts.quote: The son of Jørn Utzon, with whom he worked closely on several prestigious projects, he has completed a number of fine works of his own including the Performing Arts Centre in Esbjerg.

facts.fact: Completed in 1997, it combines a theatre and concert hall with the earlier art museum.
facts.quote: One of his most successful is the Performing Arts Centre in Esbjerg (1997) with its theatre and concert hall combined with the earlier art museum.

facts.fact: A large shared foyer serves both the concert hall and the museum, and was achieved on a modest budget.
facts.quote: Its large communal foyer catering both to the concert hall and the museum is particularly appealing and was achieved on a modest budget.

facts.fact: The Esbjerg Performing Arts Centre, 1997, is also listed among Jørn Utzon's works.
facts.quote: Esbjerg Performing Arts Centre, Esbjerg, Denmark, 1997

facts.fact: Korshagehus, just north of Rørvig in Denmark, is a Modernist summer house built in 1960 by the architect Erik Korshagen for his own use.
facts.quote: Korshagehus, situated at Korshage Fjordvej 1, just north of Rørvig, Odsherred Municipality, Denmark, is a Modernist summer house constructed in 1960 by architect Erik Korshagen for his own use.

facts.fact: He added a garage and a guesthouse in 1965 and 1984; all three buildings were listed in 1999.
facts.quote: A garage and a guesthouse were added by him in 1965 and 1984. The three buildings were listed on the Danish registry of protected buildings and places in 1999.

facts.fact: All three are built of timber with steep thatched roofs, in a Minimalist design inspired by Japanese architecture.
facts.quote: They are all constructed in timber with steep, thatched roofs to a Minimalist design with inspiration from Japanese architecture.

facts.fact: The summer house sits on top of a former coastal cliff, with the other two buildings at its foot.
facts.quote: The summer house is located on top of a former coastal cliff whereas the two other buildings are situated at the foot of it.

facts.fact: It is a single-storey timber house on poles, with cantilevered boardwalks on three sides.
facts.quote: Korshagehus is a single-storey building constructed in timber on poles with Cantilever boardwalks on three sides.

facts.fact: The house has a rectangular plan of 18 × 4 metres.
facts.quote: The house has a rectangular floor plan measuring 18 x 4 metre.

facts.fact: A central brick core with a fireplace and cupboards partly separates the large living room from the kitchen.
facts.quote: The southern portion of the building contains a large living room, partly separated from the adjacent kitchen by the central brick core with fireplace and cupboards.

facts.fact: The Röhsska Museum, also known as the Design Museum, in Gothenburg is a museum of design, fashion and applied arts.
facts.quote: The Röhsska Museum (Swedish: Röhsska museet, earlier named Röhsska konstslöjdsmuseet), also known as Design Museum, is located in Gothenburg, Sweden. It is a museum focused on design, fashion and applied arts.

facts.fact: The museum was founded in 1904, funded by a donation from the estate of Wilhelm Röhss in 1901.
facts.quote: The Röhsska Museum was founded in 1904. The financial foundation was a donation from the estate of Wilhelm Röhss in 1901, and in the ensuing years, further donations were made by people including his brother, August Röhss.

facts.fact: The original building, clad in red hand-made brick, was designed by Carl Westman in the National Romantic style.
facts.quote: The original building, clad in red, hand-made brick was designed by architect Carl Westman in the National Romantic style.

facts.fact: The museum opened to the public in 1916; its first curator, Axel Nilsson, also took part in its construction.
facts.quote: In 1916 the museum was opened to the public. The museum's first curator was Axel Nilsson, who also participated in the construction of the museum.

facts.fact: Its collection holds over 50,000 objects.
facts.quote: The museum collection consists of over 50,000 objects.

facts.fact: Carl Westman designed both the Stockholm Court House and the Röhsska Museum.
facts.quote: 1866 – Carl Westman, Swedish architect, designed the Stockholm Court House and Röhsska Museum (died 1936)

facts.fact: The Wenner-Gren Center is a tower and building complex in Vasastan, Stockholm, built 1959–1961 and opened in 1962.
facts.quote: Wenner-Gren Center is a tower and building complex in Vasastan, Stockholm, Sweden. The building was constructed 1959–1961, and opened in 1962.

facts.fact: It consists of three buildings: Pylon, a high tower; Helicon, a lower semicircular part around it; and Tetragon, a box-shaped building beside it.
facts.quote: The Center consists of three buildings named Helicon, Pylon and Tetragon. Pylon is a high tower, Helicon is a lower semicircular part surrounding the tower, and Tetragon is a box-shaped building next to the tower.

facts.fact: Helicon houses visiting scientists working at institutions in the Stockholm area.
facts.quote: Helicon contains housing for visiting scientists to institutions in the Stockholm area, and this part is owned by one of the Wenner-Gren Foundations.

facts.fact: The rest is rental space, part of it traditionally used by scientific organisations such as research-granting bodies.
facts.quote: The rest of the complex consists of commercial rental space, although some of it is traditionally used by scientific organisations, such as research-granting bodies.

facts.fact: It is named after the businessman Axel Wenner-Gren, who funded it after Nobel laureate Hugo Theorell lobbied for housing for visiting scientists.
facts.quote: The Center is named after the businessman Axel Wenner-Gren, who donated funds to finance its construction, after Nobel Prize winner Hugo Theorell had lobbied for having the housing need of visiting scientists addressed.

facts.fact: Landskrona City Hall houses the central government of Landskrona Municipality.
facts.quote: Landskrona City Hall is a city hall in Landskrona that hosts the central government of Landskrona Municipality.

facts.fact: It stands by the new harbour, near the Sofia Albertina Church and about half a kilometre east of the Landskrona Water Tower.
facts.quote: The house is located by the new harbor, near the Sofia Albertina Church and barely half a kilometer east of the Landskrona Water Tower, which is located along the city's west coast.

facts.fact: Designed by Sten Samuelson and Inge Stoltz, it was inaugurated in September 1976; an interior renovation was completed in 2021.
facts.quote: The building, designed by Sten Samuelson and Inge Stoltz, was inaugurated in September 1976 and most recently underwent an interior renovation that was completed in 2021.

facts.fact: Lillehammer Art Museum is an art gallery in Lillehammer, Norway, founded in 1921 as a gift from the merchant Einar Lunde.
facts.quote: Lillehammer Art Museum (Norwegian: Lillehammer kunstmuseum) is an art gallery located in Lillehammer, Norway. The museum was founded in 1921 as a gift from merchant Einar Lunde.

facts.fact: The older collection is mainly in the building by Erling Viksjø, completed in 1963.
facts.quote: The older part of the collection, pictures donated by Lunde and Johannessen, is mainly found in the building designed by architect Erling Viksjø, which was completed in 1963.

facts.fact: The newer building, the wing called Flygelet, was designed by Snøhetta and opened in 1992.
facts.quote: The newer building (Flygelet) was designed by the architecture firm Snøhetta and opened to the public in 1992.

facts.fact: During the 1994 Winter Olympics this building was the main venue for cultural events.
facts.quote: During the 1994 Winter Olympics, this building served as the main venue for cultural activities.

facts.fact: Stavanger Konserthus is a concert hall in Stavanger, Norway, officially opened by Crown Prince Haakon on 15 September 2012.
facts.quote: Stavanger Konserthus or Stavanger Concert Hall is a concert hall in Stavanger, Norway. It was officially opened by Crown Prince Haakon on 15 September 2012.

facts.fact: The architects were RATIO Arkitekter.
facts.quote: Architects were RATIO Arkitekter AS.

facts.fact: It has an orchestra hall and a multi-purpose hall, foyers opening to the seaside and a large outdoor amphitheatre.
facts.quote: The concert hall has two halls, an orchestra hall and a multi-purpose hall with excellent acoustics, great foyer areas out to the seaside and a large outdoor amphitheater.

facts.fact: A symphony concert and a rock concert can be held in the two halls at the same time.
facts.quote: It can be arranged symphony concert in one hall and a rock concert in the other - at the same time.

facts.fact: The orchestra hall, named after the composer Fartein Valen, is designed for acoustic music and was planned as the new home of the Stavanger Symphony Orchestra.
facts.quote: The orchestra hall is named after the composer Fartein Valen. It is specially designed for acoustic music and will become the new home of Stavanger Symphony Orchestra.

facts.fact: The orchestra hall seats 1,500 in the stalls and three galleries.
facts.quote: There are 1,500 seats in the stalls (orchestra section) and the three galleries.

facts.fact: The multi-purpose hall, named after the poet Jens Zetlitz, is designed acoustically mainly for amplified music.
facts.quote: The multi-purpose hall is named in honor of the poet and Lutheran pastor Jens Zetlitz, who was a Stavanger native. In terms of acoustics, this hall is primarily designed for amplified music.

facts.fact: It can be set up as an amphitheatre, an arena, a catwalk or a flat floor, for up to 1,700 seats.
facts.quote: It can be used for a great many purposes from rock to opera, and may be rigged as an amphitheatre, an arena, a catwalk or just have a flat floor suitable for a banquet or for a standing audience. The hall can be arranged for up to 1,700 seats.

facts.fact: Blakstad og Munthe-Kaas Arkitekter, the firm of Gudolf Blakstad and Herman Munthe-Kaas, designed Kunstnernes Hus and won the Houen Foundation Award for it in 1931.
facts.quote: The firm collaborated on several significant assignments in Norway including Kunstnernes Hus for which they were awarded the Houen Foundation Award in 1931.

facts.fact: Gudolf Blakstad is noted for work in the transition from neo-classicism to functionalism in Norwegian architecture.
facts.quote: He was noted for his work in the transition between neo-classicism and functionalism in Norwegian architecture.

facts.fact: With the Alvar Aalto Museum, Aalto's Museum of Central Finland (1961) forms a cultural centre right beside the University of Jyväskylä, also by Aalto.
facts.quote: Together with the Museum of Central Finland (Alvar Aalto, 1961), these buildings form a cultural centre in the immediate vicinity of the University of Jyväskylä (Alvar Aalto, 1951–71).

facts.fact: Both museums belong to Aalto's 'white period'.
facts.quote: Both museums represent Aalto's "white period".

facts.fact: The Museum of Central Finland's façade, rising from a hillside, shows the geometric practicality of early functionalism.
facts.quote: The ten years' difference in the design of the buildings can be seen especially in the façades — the façade of the Museum of Central Finland, rising from a slope of a hill, shows the geometric practicality of early functionalism, whereas the Aalto Museum is more closed in, but at the same time more free in its form.

facts.fact: Sähkötalo, the Electricity Building in Helsinki's Kamppi district, is the headquarters of HELEN, the city's municipal energy company.
facts.quote: Sähkötalo (lit. Electricity Building) (Swedish: Elhuset) is the name of the building located in the Kamppi district of central Helsinki, which serves as the headquarters of HELEN, the municipal energy company of the city of Helsinki.

facts.fact: The building was designed by Alvar Aalto.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Alvar Aalto.

facts.fact: Construction started in March 1970 and the building was ready on 22 January 1973.
facts.quote: Construction started in March 1970, and the building was ready for occupation on January 22, 1973.

facts.fact: It is one of only two parts of Aalto's plan for central Helsinki that were built, with Finlandia Hall; Aalto used a Miesian language of geometric grids in them.
facts.quote: Only two fragments of the overall plan were realized: the Finlandia Hall concert hall (1976) fronting on Töölö Bay and an office building in the Kamppi district for the Helsinki Electricity Company (1975). Aalto also employed the Miesian formal language of geometric grids used in those buildings for other sites in Helsinki, including the Enso-Gutzeit headquarters building (1962), the Academic Bookstore (1962), and the SYP Bank building (1969).

facts.fact: Since October 2007 its lower floors hold shops reached from Kamppi Center by an underground tunnel.
facts.quote: Since October 2007, the bottom floors of the building have been home to stores accessible from Kamppi Center by an underground pedestrian tunnel running underneath Fredrikinkatu.

facts.fact: Its window frames are lined with neon lights that slowly change colour through the night.
facts.quote: The window frames of the building are lined with neon lights that slowly change colour throughout the night.

facts.fact: Ympyrätalo in Helsinki (1968) is among the best-known works of Heikki Siren, who designed most of his buildings with his wife Kaija Siren.
facts.quote: Heikki Siren designed most of his works together with his spouse Kaija Siren. == Famous works == Finnish National Theatre Small Stage, Helsinki, 1954 Otaniemi Chapel, Espoo, 1956 Kallio Municipal Offices, Helsinki, 1965 Ympyrätalo, Helsinki, 1968

facts.fact: It is listed among Kaija Siren's major works, dated 1968.
facts.quote: 1968 Ympyrätalo, Helsinki, Finland

facts.fact: The Aalto Center, the administrative and cultural centre of Seinäjoki, is made up of six buildings by Alvar Aalto, mainly completed between 1960 and 1968.
facts.quote: Aalto Center (Finnish: Aaltokeskus) is the administrative and cultural center of the City of Seinäjoki, Finland. It comprises six buildings, designed by Alvar Aalto and mainly completed between 1960 and 1968.

facts.fact: Alvar and Elissa Aalto won the 1959 competition for a town hall that also included plans for a library, a theatre and a state office building.
facts.quote: Alvar Aalto and his wife, Elissa Aalto, won the follow-up competition in 1959, which also included plans for a library, a theatre, and a state office building.

facts.fact: The town hall was built in 1961–1962 and the library in 1964–1965.
facts.quote: The town hall was constructed in 1961–1962 and the library in 1964–1965.

facts.fact: The centre is one of Aalto's most important works, and its wooden plan is in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
facts.quote: The center represents one of Aalto's most important works and is notable in Finland and even internationally as an architectural whole. The wooden plan of the center is in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

facts.fact: Aalto also designed the courtyard between the buildings, a 'citizens' square' with a fountain and outdoor lighting.
facts.quote: Aalto also designed the courtyard between the buildings, including a fountain and the outdoor lighting. This "citizens' square" was covered with granite slabs in 1988 according to Aalto's original plans.

facts.fact: The whole centre was protected in 2005, and in July 2026 UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site with 12 other Aalto works.
facts.quote: The church was protected in 2003 by a degree from the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland central administration, and the whole center was protected in 2005 by the Ministry of the Environment. In July 2026, the Aalto Center, along with 12 other Aalto Works, was designated by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: The Finnish National Theatre stands in central Helsinki on the north side of the Central Railway Station Square.
facts.quote: The Finnish National Theatre (Finnish: Suomen Kansallisteatteri), established in 1872, is a theatre located in central Helsinki on the northern side of the Helsinki Central Railway Station Square.

facts.fact: After thirty years as a touring company, the theatre got its first permanent home in 1902, a purpose-built building next to the main railway station.
facts.quote: The theatre did not acquire a permanent home until 1902, when a purpose-built structure was erected in the heart of Helsinki, adjacent to the city's main railway station.

facts.fact: The building, completed in 1902, was designed by Onni Tarjanne in the National Romantic style.
facts.quote: The building hosting the Finnish National Theatre today was completed in 1902 and designed by architect Onni Tarjanne in the National Romantic style, inspired by romantic nationalism.

facts.fact: It has grown to hold three more stages, including the Small Stage of 1954 by Heikki and Kaija Siren.
facts.quote: In addition to the Main Stage (Suuri näyttämö), the theatre comprises the Small Stage (Pieni näyttämö) built in 1954 (by architects Heikki Siren and Kaija Siren), the Willensauna Stage built in 1976, and the Omapohja studio built in 1987.

facts.fact: The Aleksis Kivi Memorial by Wäinö Aaltonen was put up in front of the theatre in 1939.
facts.quote: In 1939, the Aleksis Kivi Memorial (designed by Wäinö Aaltonen) was erected in front of the theatre, to commemorate the Aleksis Kivi and his role in Finnish theatrical art.

facts.fact: The Finnish-language theatre was part of a cultural movement that began in the 1860s and led to independence in 1917.
facts.quote: Finnish language and art, including theatre, became the cornerstones of a cultural movement which began in the 1860s, gradually developing political ambitions by the turn of the century, and eventually leading to national independence in 1917.

facts.fact: Uspenski Cathedral is the largest Orthodox church in Northern Europe.
facts.quote: It is the largest Orthodox church in Northern Europe.

facts.fact: It was designed by the Russian architect Aleksey Gornostayev and built after his death, in 1862–1868, under architect Ivan Varnek.
facts.quote: The cathedral designed by the Russian architect Aleksey Gornostayev (1808–1862). The cathedral was built after his death in 1862–1868 and the work was led by architect Ivan Varnek.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 25 October 1868.
facts.quote: It was inaugurated on 25 October 1868.

facts.fact: Its 700,000 bricks came by barge from the Bomarsund Fortress, demolished in the Crimean War.
facts.quote: Used in construction of the cathedral, 700 000 bricks were brought over in barges from the Bomarsund Fortress that had been demolished in the Crimean War.

facts.fact: The cathedral stands on a hillside on the Katajanokka peninsula, overlooking the city.
facts.quote: The cathedral is set upon a hillside on the Katajanokka peninsula overlooking the city.

facts.fact: Gornostayev was a pioneer of the Russian Revival, credited with reviving the tented roofs of the Russian North.
facts.quote: He is credited with the rebirth of traditional tented roof architecture of Russian North.

facts.fact: The cathedral was Gornostayev's last work, completed after his death.
facts.quote: His last work, Orthodox Uspenski Cathedral in Helsinki, was completed after his death.

facts.fact: Tampere Hall is the largest congress centre in the Nordic countries, at the southern edge of Sorsapuisto park in central Tampere.
facts.quote: The Tampere Hall (Finnish: Tampere-talo; Swedish: Tammerforshuset) is the largest congress centre in the Nordic countries, located in the southern edge of Sorsapuisto, in the centre of Tampere, Finland.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 29 September 1990.
facts.quote: It was inaugurated on September 29, 1990.

facts.fact: Esa Piironen and Sakari Aartelo designed it, from a first-prize competition entry, as a concert and congress hall for 2,000 people.
facts.quote: In 1978 Esa Piironen established a new office with Sakari Aartelo. Their main work is Tampere Hall (a concert and congress hall for 2000 persons) based on a 1st prize competition entry.

facts.fact: The main auditorium seats 1,756.
facts.quote: The seating capacity of the main auditorium is 1,756.

facts.fact: The University of Tampere's main building stands opposite, and the railway station is half a kilometre away.
facts.quote: Opposite of the Tampere Hall is the main building of the University of Tampere, and the Tampere railway station is only half a kilometre away.

facts.fact: The Tampere Opera and the Tampere Philharmonic Orchestra are based there.
facts.quote: The Tampere Opera and the Tampere Philharmonic Orchestra are also based there.

facts.fact: The Moomin Museum moved into the complex in 2017.
facts.quote: In 2017, the Moomin Museum moved into the complex.

facts.fact: Muurame church in central Finland was designed by Alvar Aalto and completed in 1929.
facts.quote: Muurame church, located in Muurame, central Finland, was designed by the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto, and completed in 1929.

facts.fact: It was Aalto's first church and the only one of his 1920s church designs to be built, marking his move from Nordic Classicism to Functionalism.
facts.quote: It was the first Aalto-designed church, and the only one of his many church designs in the 1920s, to be built, and represents his transition from Nordic Classicism to the Functionalist style he is mostly known for.

facts.fact: Critics have often undervalued it as a transitional work, and Aalto himself called it his 'aberration of youth'.
facts.quote: As a transitional work, the Muurame church has been undervalued among Aalto's designs by many critics, and even the architect himself called it his 'aberration of youth' (nuoruudensynti).

facts.fact: Its long single-aisle nave and campanile were influenced by the churches Aalto saw on his honeymoon in Italy.
facts.quote: The church's elongated-nave, single-aisle design and campanile (belfry) were influenced by Aalto's honeymoon trip to Italy a few years earlier, and the churches he saw there.

facts.fact: The church was fully restored to its original design in 2016.
facts.quote: The church was comprehensively restored in 2016 to its original design.

facts.fact: The restoration brought back the original colours, a bright blue and red ceiling and dark grey fixtures, in place of white and light wood.
facts.quote: Most notably, the interior colour scheme was changed from its pre-renovation white and light wood — often associated with Aalto's minimalist style — to the original, more colourful one, consisting of bright blue and red ceiling and dark grey fixtures.

facts.fact: The Seinäjoki Civil Guard House is one of the first public buildings designed entirely by Alvar Aalto and is considered one of his breakthrough works.
facts.quote: It is notable for being one of the first public buildings designed entirely by the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto, and is considered one of his breakthrough works.

facts.fact: Aalto designed it in 1924–1926 as the regional headquarters of the Civil Guard militia and the Lotta Svärd women's auxiliary.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Aalto in 1924–1926, to serve as the headquarters of the South Ostrobothnia division of the Finnish Civil Guard (aka. White Guard, or Defence Corps) voluntary militia and the related Lotta Svärd women's auxiliary organisation.

facts.fact: In the Nordic Classical style, it is one of the main works of Aalto's early neoclassical period, before his modernism.
facts.quote: The design, in the Nordic classical style, is considered one of the main works from Aalto's earlier neoclassical period, predating the modernist style for which he is more widely known.

facts.fact: The complex is three buildings around an enclosed courtyard.
facts.quote: The building complex consists of three buildings and a courtyard enclosed by them.

facts.fact: The three-storey main building has a masonry ground floor and timber upper floors.
